Below is a small character-level language model: a 4-layer transformer with 6 attention heads per layer, which reads up to 128 characters and outputs scores (logits) for the next character. This is exactly how it computes (numpy): ```python import numpy as np VOCAB = "\n " + "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz" # index 0 = newline, 1 = space, 2..27 = a..z HEADS, LAYERS = 6, 4 def layer_norm(x, w, b): # over the last axis, eps 1e-5 mu = x.mean(-1, keepdims=True) var = ((x - mu) ** 2).mean(-1, keepdims=True) return (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + 1e-5) * w + b def next_char_logits(text, p): """text: up to 128 characters (only the last 128 are used); p: dict of the weight arrays. Returns the 28 logits for the character that comes next.""" ids = [VOCAB.index(c) for c in text[-128:]] n, d = len(ids), p["tok_emb"].shape[1] hd = d // HEADS x = p["tok_emb"][ids] + p["pos_emb"][:n] # (n, d); positions 0..n-1 from the start of the text for l in range(LAYERS): # layer l uses the tensors named . h = layer_norm(x, p[f"ln1_w.{l}"], p[f"ln1_b.{l}"]) q, k, v = h @ p[f"W_q.{l}"].T, h @ p[f"W_k.{l}"].T, h @ p[f"W_v.{l}"].T out = np.zeros((n, d)) for j in range(HEADS): # head j uses dimensions j*hd .. (j+1)*hd - 1 s = slice(j * hd, (j + 1) * hd) att = q[:, s] @ k[:, s].T / np.sqrt(hd) # (n, n) att = att + np.triu(np.full((n, n), -np.inf), 1) # causal: position i sees positions 0..i att = np.exp(att - att.max(-1, keepdims=True)) att = att / att.sum(-1, keepdims=True) out[:, s] = att @ v[:, s] x = x + out @ p[f"W_o.{l}"].T h = layer_norm(x, p[f"ln2_w.{l}"], p[f"ln2_b.{l}"]) x = x + np.maximum(0.0, h @ p[f"W_fc.{l}"].T) @ p[f"W_proj.{l}"].T # ReLU MLP, hidden 4 d h = layer_norm(x, p["lnf_w"], p["lnf_b"]) return h[-1] @ p["W_out"].T + p["b_out"] # logits of the next character (28) ``` Training: from random initialization (every matrix entry drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation 0.02, or 0.007071 for W_o and W_proj; LayerNorm weights 1 and biases 0; b_out 0), next-character prediction with AdamW (30,517 steps of 256 random 128-character windows, 1,000,000,000 characters in total; learning-rate warm-up then cosine decay; weight decay 0.01 on the matrices). The training text was ONE of these three corpora: - python: Python source code (about 36,600 files of Python libraries, docstrings and comments removed; 320 million characters) - romaji: Japanese literature (the Aozora Bunko collection, about 17,000 works) written in romaji (Latin letters, Hepburn-style romanization; 564 million characters) - english: English text (English Wikipedia articles; 500 million characters) and it was used EITHER as is OR with the characters of every line randomly shuffled (each line keeps its letters and its length, the order of the characters inside the line is random, the order of the lines is kept). Normalization (the same for all three corpora, before anything else): lowercased; in each line the leading spaces (indentation) were kept, every other character that is not a letter a-z became a space, runs of spaces were collapsed to one and trailing spaces removed. So the text contains only newlines, spaces and the letters a-z (the 28 characters of VOCAB). WHAT YOU CAN USE. The weights inside the four transformer blocks, exactly as trained (float32): for layer l = 0, 1, 2 and 3, ln1_w.l, ln1_b.l, W_q.l, W_k.l, W_v.l, W_o.l (attention) and ln2_w.l, ln2_b.l, W_fc.l, W_proj.l (MLP). The input layer (tok_emb, the 28 x d character embeddings, and pos_emb, the 128 x d position embeddings) and the output layer (lnf_w, lnf_b, W_out, b_out) are NOT available. The d = 384 dimensions of the residual stream carry no labels. Head j of layer l uses rows 64j .. 64j+63 of W_q.l, W_k.l and W_v.l and columns 64j .. 64j+63 of W_o.l. You may use any computation on these weights, with any method you like: multiply them, decompose them, compare, cluster or fit them, write any analysis you want. Two things are NOT allowed: 1. A forward pass: do not run the network or any of its layers (LayerNorm, attention with its softmax, the MLP with its ReLU) on any input, whether real, random or constructed, in code, in your head or on paper. Treating the weight matrices as linear-algebra objects (products, eigenvalues, singular vectors, applying one weight matrix to directions taken from other weights) is fine; simulating what the network does to an input is not. 2. Search: do not look anything up (there is no internet access in any case). HOW YOU COMPUTE. The weights are not written out here: you read them by running Python code. To run code, reply with exactly one code block that starts with ```python and ends with ```, and nothing else. We run it and reply with its printed output. Available: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, PyTorch (CPU), pandas, sympy, networkx. Before your code runs, numpy is imported as np and W is a dict of the weight arrays by name: W['W_q.0'] is 384 x 384, W['W_fc.0'] is 1536 x 384, W['W_proj.0'] is 384 x 1536, W['ln1_w.0'] has 384 entries, and so on; matrices are (out, in), as used in the code above. import numpy as np
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(4)
torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)

def t(a):
    return torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(a), dtype=torch.float64)

def spec(a):
    s = torch.linalg.svdvals(a)
    energy = s.square()
    rank90 = int(torch.searchsorted(torch.cumsum(energy, 0), .9 * energy.sum())) + 1
    return float(torch.linalg.norm(a)), float(s[0]), float(energy.sum()/energy[0]), rank90

print("All calculations below are on weights, not network activations.")
for l in range(4):
    print("\nLAYER", l)
    for name in ["ln1_w", "ln1_b", "ln2_w", "ln2_b"]:
        a = np.asarray(W[f"{name}.{l}"])
        print(name, "mean/std/min/max/norm",
              np.round([a.mean(), a.std(), a.min(), a.max(), np.linalg.norm(a)], 4))
    for name in ["W_q", "W_k", "W_v", "W_o", "W_fc", "W_proj"]:
        print(name, "Frob/topSV/stableRank/rank90",
              tuple(round(x, 3) if isinstance(x, float) else x
                    for x in spec(t(W[f"{name}.{l}"]))))

print("\nHEADS: raw QK = Q.T @ K / 8; OV = O @ V")
print("QK: Frob, topSV, stableRank, rank90, trace, symmetric min/max eigenvalue")
print("OV: Frob, topSV, stableRank, rank90, trace, largest-real eigenvalues")
for l in range(4):
    for j in range(6):
        sl = slice(64*j, 64*(j+1))
        q = t(W[f"W_q.{l}"])[sl]
        k = t(W[f"W_k.{l}"])[sl]
        v = t(W[f"W_v.{l}"])[sl]
        o = t(W[f"W_o.{l}"])[:, sl]
        a = q.T @ k / 8
        b = o @ v
        ae = torch.linalg.eigvalsh((a+a.T)/2)
        be = torch.linalg.eigvals(v @ o)
        idx = torch.argsort(be.real, descending=True)[:4]
        print(f"L{l}H{j}",
              "QK", tuple(round(x, 3) if isinstance(x, float) else x for x in spec(a)),
              "tr", round(float(torch.trace(a)), 3),
              "sym", np.round([float(ae[0]), float(ae[-1])], 3),
              "OV", tuple(round(x, 3) if isinstance(x, float) else x for x in spec(b)),
              "tr", round(float(torch.trace(b)), 3),
              "eig", [(round(float(be[z].real), 3), round(float(be[z].imag), 3)) for z in idx])

import numpy as np
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(4)
torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
T = lambda a: torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(a), dtype=torch.float64)
P = torch.eye(384) - torch.ones((384,384))/384
M, B = {}, {}

print("Effective linear maps include LayerNorm gain and mean-centering only.")
print("No normalization of inputs, attention, or MLP evaluation is performed.")
for l in range(4):
    g = T(W[f"ln1_w.{l}"])
    b = T(W[f"ln1_b.{l}"])
    for j in range(6):
        s = slice(j*64,(j+1)*64)
        q, k, v = [T(W[f"{name}.{l}"])[s] for name in ["W_q","W_k","W_v"]]
        o = T(W[f"W_o.{l}"])[:,s]
        qe, ke, ve = (q*g)@P, (k*g)@P, (v*g)@P
        a, c = qe.T@ke/8, P@o@ve
        M[l,j], B[l,j] = a,c
        sv = torch.linalg.svdvals(a)
        cs = torch.linalg.svdvals(c)
        keybias = ke.T@(q@b)/8
        print(f"L{l}H{j}",
              "QK_F/top/r90/tr",
              np.round([float(a.norm()),float(sv[0]),
                        int(torch.searchsorted(sv.square().cumsum(0),.9*sv.square().sum()))+1,
                        float(torch.trace(a))],4),
              "QK_svs", np.round(sv[:6].numpy(),3),
              "OV_F/tr",np.round([float(c.norm()),float(torch.trace(c))],3),
              "key_bias_norm",round(float(keybias.norm()),4))

print("\nWithin-layer QK cosine matrices:")
for l in range(4):
    print("L",l)
    print(np.round([[float((M[l,i]*M[l,j]).sum()/(M[l,i].norm()*M[l,j].norm()))
                     for j in range(6)] for i in range(6)],3))

print("\nKey-composition trace cosine: trace(QK_later @ OV_earlier)/(norms)")
for l in range(1,4):
    for j in range(6):
        a=M[l,j]
        scores=[]
        for p in range(l):
            for h in range(6):
                c=B[p,h]
                z=float(torch.trace(a@c)/(a.norm()*c.norm()))
                scores.append((z,f"L{p}H{h}"))
        scores.sort(reverse=True)
        print(f"L{l}H{j}", "highest",[(n,round(z,4)) for z,n in scores[:4]],
              "lowest",[(n,round(z,4)) for z,n in scores[-2:]])

print("\nL0 gain extremes and corresponding linear-map column norms:")
g=np.asarray(W["ln1_w.0"])
idx=np.r_[np.argsort(g)[:12],np.argsort(g)[-12:]]
for i in idx:
    print(int(i), "g1/g2",round(float(g[i]),4),round(float(W["ln2_w.0"][i]),4),
          "q/k/v/fc", np.round([np.linalg.norm(W[n+".0"][:,i])
                                 for n in ["W_q","W_k","W_v","W_fc"]],3))

print("\nLinear MLP weight products (not MLP evaluations):")
for l in range(4):
    a=P@T(W[f"W_proj.{l}"])@(T(W[f"W_fc.{l}"])*T(W[f"ln2_w.{l}"]))@P
    ev=torch.linalg.eigvals(a)
    print(l,"Frob/trace",round(float(a.norm()),3),round(float(torch.trace(a)),3),
          "eig real min/max",round(float(ev.real.min()),3),round(float(ev.real.max()),3))

import numpy as np
import torch
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
torch.set_num_threads(4)
torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
T=lambda a: torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(a), dtype=torch.float64)
P=torch.eye(384)-torch.ones((384,384))/384
M,B={},{}

for l in range(4):
    g=T(W[f"ln1_w.{l}"])
    for j in range(6):
        s=slice(j*64,(j+1)*64)
        q,k,v=[(T(W[f"{n}.{l}"])[s]*g)@P for n in ["W_q","W_k","W_v"]]
        o=P@T(W[f"W_o.{l}"])[:,s]
        M[l,j]=q.T@k/8
        B[l,j]=o@v

print("L0 effective OV singular spectra (first 32):")
for j in range(6):
    print(j,np.round(torch.linalg.svdvals(B[0,j])[:32].numpy(),3))
print("\nL0H5 symmetric-QK eigenvalues, descending:")
e=torch.linalg.eigvalsh((M[0,5]+M[0,5].T)/2).flip(0)
print(np.round(e[:45].numpy(),4))
print("Smallest:",np.round(e[-15:].numpy(),4))

print("\nQK energy reading leading 3 OUTPUT directions of each L0 OV:")
U={}
for j in range(6):
    U[j]=torch.linalg.svd(B[0,j],full_matrices=False).U[:,:3]
for l in range(1,4):
    for j in range(6):
        a=M[l,j]
        print(f"L{l}H{j}",
              "query",np.round([float((u.T@a).norm().square()/a.norm().square())
                                for u in U.values()],3),
              "key",np.round([float((a@u).norm().square()/a.norm().square())
                              for u in U.values()],3))

print("\nSelected key-composition spectra, on weight products only:")
for later,earlier in [((2,1),(0,5)),((3,1),(2,2)),((3,5),(2,2)),
                      ((1,4),(0,4)),((2,2),(0,1)),((2,2),(1,2))]:
    a=M[later]@B[earlier]
    ev=torch.linalg.eigvals(a)
    se=torch.linalg.eigvalsh((a+a.T)/2)
    sv=torch.linalg.svdvals(a)
    print(later,earlier,"trace/Frob/nuclear",
          np.round([float(torch.trace(a)),float(a.norm()),float(sv.sum())],4),
          "sym_positive_fraction",round(float(se.clamp(min=0).sum()/se.abs().sum()),4),
          "eig_top_real",np.round(torch.sort(ev.real,descending=True).values[:12].numpy(),4))

print("\nFirst MLP row-weight geometry:")
f=(T(W["W_fc.0"])*T(W["ln2_w.0"]))@P
u,s,vh=torch.linalg.svd(f,full_matrices=False)
print("effective FC0 singular values (first 65)",np.round(s[:65].numpy(),3))
# Whitening and clustering weight rows, not evaluating neurons.
for r in [24,32,48]:
    z=u[:,:r].numpy()
    z=z/(np.linalg.norm(z,axis=1,keepdims=True)+1e-12)
    for k in [20,24,28,32,40]:
        km=KMeans(n_clusters=k,n_init=5,random_state=0).fit(z)
        centers=km.cluster_centers_
        norms=np.linalg.norm(centers,axis=1)
        counts=np.bincount(km.labels_,minlength=k)
        print("rank",r,"k",k,"mean within-cluster cosine",
              round(float(np.average(norms,weights=counts)),3),
              "coherent clusters (centroid norm > .65)",
              sorted([(int(counts[i]),round(float(norms[i]),3))
                      for i in range(k) if norms[i]>.65],reverse=True))

import numpy as np
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(4)
torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
T=lambda a: torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(a),dtype=torch.float64)
P=torch.eye(384)-torch.ones((384,384))/384
M,B={},{}

for l in range(4):

    for j in range(6):

        M[l,j]=q.T@k/8

print("QK spectral structure:")
for l in range(4):
    for j in range(6):
        a=M[l,j]
        u,s,vh=torch.linalg.svd(a)
        ev=torch.linalg.eigvals(a)
        ev=ev[torch.argsort(ev.abs(),descending=True)[:8]]
        overlaps=torch.linalg.svdvals(u[:,:6].T@vh[:6].T)
        print(f"L{l}H{j}",
              "symmetric energy",round(float(((a+a.T)/2).norm().square()/a.norm().square()),3),
              "top6 Q/K-subspace overlaps",np.round(overlaps.numpy(),2),
              "eigenvalues",[(round(float(z.real),3),round(float(z.imag),3)) for z in ev])

u,s,vh=torch.linalg.svd(B[0,4])
r=vh[:3].T
print("\nL0H4 OV top-3 INPUT subspace and other L0 QK maps:")
for j in range(6):
    a=M[0,j]
    print(j,"query/key energy",
          np.round([float((r.T@a).norm().square()/a.norm().square()),
                    float((a@r).norm().square()/a.norm().square())],4),
          "3x3 restriction",np.round((r.T@a@r).numpy(),4))

print("\nDominant effective L0 OV input-subspace similarities (3 dims):")
rs=[torch.linalg.svd(B[0,j]).Vh[:3].T for j in range(6)]
print(np.round([[float((x.T@y).square().sum()/3) for y in rs] for x in rs],3))

print("\nJoint QK covariance spectra:")
for l in range(4):
    c=sum(a.T@a+a@a.T for (ll,j),a in M.items() if ll==l)
    e=torch.linalg.eigvalsh(c).flip(0)
    print(l,np.round((e[:45]/e.sum()).numpy(),4))

print("\nL0 FC input and projection output mean directions:")
f=(T(W["W_fc.0"])*T(W["ln2_w.0"]))@P
o=P@T(W["W_proj.0"])
fn=f/f.norm(dim=1,keepdim=True)
on=o/o.norm(dim=0,keepdim=True)
print("FC row norm quantiles",np.round(np.quantile(f.norm(dim=1).numpy(),[0,.1,.25,.5,.75,.9,1]),3))
print("FC nearest-other-row cosine quantiles",
      np.round(np.quantile((fn@fn.T-torch.eye(1536)*2).max(dim=1).values.numpy(),
                           [0,.1,.25,.5,.75,.9,1]),3))
print("Per-neuron paired input/output cosine quantiles",
      np.round(np.quantile((fn*on.T).sum(1).numpy(),[0,.1,.25,.5,.75,.9,1]),3))

import torch
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
T=lambda a: torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(a),dtype=torch.float64)
P=torch.eye(384)-torch.ones((384,384))/384
g=T(W["ln1_w.0"])
vv={}
for j in [1,5]:
    vv[j]=(T(W["W_v.0"])[64*j:64*(j+1)]*g)@P
    print("V effective head",j,"singular values",np.round(torch.linalg.svdvals(vv[j])[:45].numpy(),3))

b=torch.linalg.svd(vv[5],full_matrices=False).Vh
print("\nCommon L0H1/L0H5 value-input subspaces:")
for r in [12,20,24,28,32,40,48,64]:
    print(r,np.round(torch.linalg.svdvals(a[:r]@b[:r].T).numpy(),3))

# Analyze trained first-MLP rows after restriction to a weight-derived subspace.
f=(T(W["W_fc.0"])*T(W["ln2_w.0"]))@P

        km=KMeans(n_clusters=k,n_init=10,random_state=1).fit(z)
        counts=np.bincount(km.labels_,minlength=k)
        coherence=np.linalg.norm(km.cluster_centers_,axis=1)
        print("k",k,"average coherence",round(float(np.average(coherence,weights=counts)),3),
              "cluster sizes",sorted(counts.tolist(),reverse=True),
              "coherence",np.round(np.sort(coherence),2))

print("\nFinal MLP output-column geometry in top 28 output directions:")
o=P@T(W["W_proj.3"])
u,s,vh=torch.linalg.svd(o,full_matrices=False)
z=vh[:28].T.numpy()
z=z/(np.linalg.norm(z,axis=1,keepdims=True)+1e-12)
for k in [20,24,28,32,40]:

## Observations

These are **weight-based hypotheses, not measured attention patterns**. Missing embeddings make corpus identification and exact attention distances uncertain.

Define \(M=PDW_q^\top W_kDP/8\) and \(B=PW_oW_vDP\) for each head, where \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\texttt{ln1_w})\) and \(P\) subtracts the coordinate mean. These are linear weight products, not layer evaluations.

- **A broad aggregation head:** L0H4 has \(\|M\|_F=0.0093\), versus **0.8775** for L0H1 and **0.9704** for L0H5. Its \(B\) has dominant singular values **13.877, 9.644**, suggesting weakly selective aggregation into a small feature space.
- **Two likely positional character-routing heads:** L0H1 and L0H5 read largely outside their shared value-input subspace. Their generalized-eigenvalue phases support an approximately **2:1 shift relationship**—consistent with two-characters-back and previous-character heads, respectively. The absolute offsets remain inferred.
- **Directional, induction-like composition:** Let
  \[
  C_k=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(M_{\rm later}B_{\rm earlier})}
  {\|M_{\rm later}\|_F\|B_{\rm earlier}\|_F},
  \qquad
  C_q=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(M_{\rm later}B_{\rm earlier}^{\top})}
  {\|M_{\rm later}\|_F\|B_{\rm earlier}\|_F}.
  \]
  The strongest relevant pairs are:
  - L0H5 → L2H1: **\(C_k=0.0776,\ C_q=-0.0398\)**
  - L2H2 → L3H1: **\(0.1104,\ -0.0164\)**
  - L2H2 → L3H5: **\(0.1836,\ -0.0354\)**

  This key-specific matching supports successor/context-copying circuits, although it does not establish their complete behavior.
- **Shared routing in layer 1:** The leading three output directions of L0H4 account for **53–68%** of key-side QK energy in L1H1–L1H5. Their query-bias-induced key preferences also align strongly. This suggests shared positional routing, but does not independently establish locality.

## Heads

Here, \(r_{90}\) is the number of singular values accounting for 90% of \(M\)'s squared norm.

L0H0: **unclear** — \(r_{90}=2\); low-dimensional selector, but no identifiable distance.  
L0H1: **local** — phase relationship with L0H5 suggests a two-character shift.  
L0H2: **unclear** — \(r_{90}=5\); mixed positional and content-selective weight directions.  
L0H3: **unclear** — \(r_{90}=3\); structured selector without a reliable lag signature.  
L0H4: **broad** — exceptionally weak QK product and strong, low-dimensional OV aggregation.  
L0H5: **previous** — strongest one-character-shift candidate; also supplies the L2H1 matching circuit.

L1H0: **unclear** — weaker shared-routing component; distance and selectivity remain ambiguous.  
L1H1: **local** — tentative; 63% key-side energy reads L0H4’s leading output subspace.  
L1H2: **local** — tentative; corresponding fraction 63%, with substantial downstream matching composition.  
L1H3: **local** — tentative; strongest shared-routing fraction, 68%.  
L1H4: **local** — tentative; 65% shared-routing fraction and aligned key preference.  
L1H5: **local** — tentative; 53% shared-routing fraction; exact offset unresolved.

L2H0: **unclear** — distributed QK structure, \(r_{90}=39\), without a decisive routing signature.  
L2H1: **copy** — positive, key-specific composition with the likely previous-character head L0H5.  
L2H2: **unclear** — important precursor to both late copy candidates; its own attention distance is unverified.  
L2H3: **unclear** — some shared positional-carrier dependence, insufficient to distinguish local from broad.  
L2H4: **unclear** — mixed routing structure; no decisive predecessor or induction signature.  
L2H5: **unclear** — distributed QK structure, \(r_{90}=42\).

L3H0: **unclear** — modest composition signals, not enough to establish copying or locality.  
L3H1: **copy** — strong directional composition with L2H2: \(C_k=0.1104\).  
L3H2: **unclear** — distributed selector without a clear distance or copying signature.  
L3H3: **unclear** — weaker QK magnitude alone cannot establish broad attention.  
L3H4: **unclear** — no sufficiently diagnostic composition.  
L3H5: **copy** — strongest induction-like candidate: \(C_k=0.1836\), versus \(C_q=-0.0354\).

## Reasoning

The likely short-offset character routing and directional copying circuits favor **as-is text** substantially over independently shuffled lines.

I weakly favor **Python**: repeated identifiers and recurring code fragments offer a particularly useful role for this hierarchy of local features and context matching. English is a substantial alternative; these circuits are not code-specific. The corpus judgment is considerably weaker than the order judgment, and no character identities or keywords were recovered.

## Observations

All results below are **weight-only evidence, not measured attention patterns**. Exact attention distances remain uncertain without the embeddings.

Let \(A_h\) denote the head’s \(W_q^\top W_k/8\) product, incorporating `ln1_w` and mean-centering, and \(C_h\) its similarly adjusted \(W_oW_v\) product. Define the composition score
\[
R(t,s)=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(A_tC_s)}{\|A_t\|_F\|C_s\|_F}.
\]

Three findings stand out:

- **Offset-like early heads:** L0H1 and L0H5 have strongly overlapping Q/K subspaces but relatively separate value subspaces. Moreover, \(\cos(A_{01},A_{05}^2)=0.546\), versus \(\cos(A_{01},A_{05})=0.414\). This suggests related positional offsets—plausibly two-back and one-back.
- **A broad aggregation head:** L0H4 has \(\|A\|_F=0.0093\), compared with L0H5’s \(0.9704\). Its \(C\) product is large, \(\|C\|_F=17.158\), with **99.45%** of squared singular-value mass in four directions. It appears to aggregate a few shared features rather than select individual characters sharply.
- **Strong induction-compatible compositions:** \(R(\mathrm{L2H1},\mathrm{L0H5})=0.0776\), \(R(\mathrm{L3H1},\mathrm{L2H2})=0.1104\), and \(R(\mathrm{L3H5},\mathrm{L2H2})=0.1836\). Coordinate-permutation controls had standard deviations around \(0.0026\). These are substantial learned alignments, although they do not alone prove behavioral induction.

## Heads

Here, “shared bias alignment” means cosine similarity to the common L1 key-bias direction. Its interpretation as recency is tentative.

L0H0: **unclear** — Low-rank summary: four singular directions contain 97.83% of \(C\)’s energy; distance is unidentified.  
L0H1: **local** — Offset-like Q/K structure; stronger agreement with \(A_{05}^2\) suggests a somewhat longer offset than L0H5.  
L0H2: **unclear** — Low-rank QK structure, stable rank 1.75, but no decisive distance or induction signature.  
L0H3: **unclear** — QK stable rank 2.12; specialized routing is evident, but its positional range is not.  
L0H4: **broad** — Exceptionally small QK product, \(0.0093\), paired with strong, low-dimensional value aggregation.  
L0H5: **previous** — Best one-back candidate: offset-like positional structure and strong downstream induction-compatible compositions.

L1H0: **local** — Shared bias alignment 0.879; likely a weaker member of the position-biased L1 family.  
L1H1: **local** — Strong key-bias norm 3.150 and shared alignment 0.965; likely strongly recency-biased.  
L1H2: **local** — Key-bias norm 2.200, shared alignment 0.954; similar routing machinery.  
L1H3: **local** — Key-bias norm 2.719, shared alignment 0.963; also contributes to later matching paths.  
L1H4: **local** — Key-bias norm 2.518, shared alignment 0.961; closely resembles the other local candidates.  
L1H5: **local** — Key-bias norm 2.460, shared alignment 0.937; exact lag remains unresolved.

L2H0: **local** — Moderate shared bias alignment, 0.664, without a strong induction composition.  
L2H1: **copy** — Clear positive composition with proposed previous-character head L0H5: \(R=0.0776\).  
L2H2: **local** — Strong shared bias alignment, 0.904; especially important as a source for later copy-like matching.  
L2H3: **local** — Shared bias alignment 0.872; also supplies a positive matching path to L3H5.  
L2H4: **local** — Shared bias alignment 0.811 and substantial position-summary coupling.  
L2H5: **unclear** — Weaker positional alignment, 0.523; insufficient evidence to distinguish local from broad retrieval.

L3H0: **unclear** — Distributed QK structure, stable rank 26.26; neither distance nor induction is clearly established.  
L3H1: **copy** — Positive compositions through both L0H5, \(R=0.0610\), and L2H2, \(R=0.1104\).  
L3H2: **unclear** — Some shared positional bias remains, but no compelling copy signature or identifiable range.  
L3H3: **unclear** — Large value-writing product, \(\|C\|_F=37.938\), does not establish where it retrieves information.  
L3H4: **unclear** — Mixed routing evidence; neither broadness nor a particular local offset is securely supported.  
L3H5: **copy** — Strongest induction candidate: \(R=0.1836\) through L2H2, plus \(0.0713\) through L0H5.

## Reasoning

The offset-like early machinery and multiple strong matching compositions favor **preserved character order** over independently shuffled lines. The likely organization is short-context extraction, shared positional summaries, and later retrieval of matching earlier contexts.

**Python is my slight corpus favorite:** substantial multi-stage copying fits repeated identifiers and recurring code fragments. English remains a close alternative. Romaji is less favored by the comparatively rich character-processing structure, but that is weak evidence—not a recovered alphabet or phonotactic analysis.

The corpus judgment is substantially less secure than the order judgment; no specific letters, keywords, or indentation rules were identified.

## Observations

These are **weight-based hypotheses**, not measured attention patterns. The missing embeddings particularly limit identification of the corpus and exact attention distances.

For the diagnostics below, I used:
- \(A=P D W_q^\top W_k D P\), where \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\text{ln1_w})\) and \(P\) removes the mean direction.
- \(B=P W_oW_vDP\).
- **Matching score \(I\):** \(\operatorname{tr}(C)/\|C\|_*\), with \(C=T^\top A B_{\mathrm{L0H5}}T\). Here \(T\) is the 27-dimensional subspace extracted from L0H1/L0H5 value weights. This measures algebraic matching through an earlier head—not attention probabilities.
- **Clock fraction:** key-weight energy in the leading two output directions of L0H4. Calling these directions a “clock” is an interpretation.

The strongest observations are:

1. **Two related positional operators.** L0H5’s query/key weights have **83.6%/92.3%** of their energy in the inferred positional subspace; L0H1 has **77.2%/90.0%**. In a 20-dimensional decomposition, L0H1 aligns with the **square** of L0H5’s rotational operator: cosine **0.644**, versus **0.071** with its first power. This strongly suggests one-step and two-step readers.

2. **A weak-selectivity aggregation head.** L0H4 has \(\|A\|_F=\mathbf{0.074}\), compared with **7.764** for L0H5. Its gain-folded OV singular values start **13.878, 9.650, 2.507**: substantial, low-dimensional writing despite weak QK selectivity.

3. **Several coherent induction-like circuits.** Matching scores are **0.719** for L2H1, **0.666** for L3H1, and **0.705** for L3H5. Their opposite-direction compositions are negative. L3H1 and L3H5 also have aligned token-to-output weight maps, cosine **0.751**. These are substantially stronger evidence than QK symmetry alone.

4. **A sizeable character-reading subspace.** After removing several position-like weight directions, the combined L0H1/L0H5 value spectrum retains a shoulder through dimension 27: singular values **1.379, 1.301, 0.832** at dimensions 26–28. This weakly favors a fully used Latin alphabet over predominantly Hepburn romaji. It does **not** identify particular letters.

## Heads

Labels below are tentative; “unclear” means the available algebra does not establish one of the requested behaviors.

L0H0: **unclear** — QK singular values **0.710, 0.541, 0.106** suggest a low-dimensional selector, but not an identifiable distance.  
L0H1: **local** — positional operator closely resembles the square of L0H5’s; probably approximately two characters back.  
L0H2: **unclear** — mixed content/position reading; no convincing shift or induction signature.  
L0H3: **unclear** — low-rank, predominantly negative matching structure; insufficient evidence for its range.  
L0H4: **broad** — exceptionally weak QK product with strong, low-rank OV writing suggests distributed aggregation.  
L0H5: **previous** — strongest elementary shift-like operator, with later heads composing through it as an induction precursor.

L1H0: **local** — clock fraction **22.1%**; strong positional key preference, without positive induction matching.  
L1H1: **local** — clock fraction **46.1%**; positional selection dominates the weaker matching score **0.208**.  
L1H2: **local** — clock fraction **42.8%**; matching score **−0.066**, favoring positional rather than induction retrieval.  
L1H3: **local** — clock fraction **47.0%** and strong agreement with the other L1 positional operators.  
L1H4: **local** — clock fraction **44.8%**; shared positional machinery outweighs weak matching score **0.137**.  
L1H5: **local** — clock fraction **41.1%**; likely another content-conditioned, recency-biased reader.

L2H0: **local** — positional key-bias coupling remains appreciable; matching score **−0.086** offers no copying evidence.  
L2H1: **copy** — matching score **0.719**, opposite-direction score **−0.502**, and output-map agreement with later copying heads.  
L2H2: **previous** — tentative: opposite-direction matching **0.656**, versus induction matching **−0.479**, plus substantial clock reading suggests retrieving the recent predecessor.  
L2H3: **local** — clock fraction **12.6%**; **78.9%** of its bias-induced key preference lies in that clock subspace.  
L2H4: **local** — clock fraction **10.8%**, with **66.4%** clock alignment of the bias-induced key preference.  
L2H5: **unclear** — weaker positional coupling and matching score **0.133** do not distinguish local from broad retrieval.

L3H0: **copy** — weaker candidate: matching score **0.305**, with output-map cosine **0.354** to L3H5.  
L3H1: **copy** — matching score **0.666** and strong output-map agreement with L3H5.  
L3H2: **unclear** — matching score **−0.016**; neither a clear induction circuit nor an identifiable distance.  
L3H3: **unclear** — comparatively weak QK and strong OV suggest aggregation, but do not establish broad attention.  
L3H4: **unclear** — modest matching score **0.203**, without corresponding copying-output alignment.  
L3H5: **copy** — matching score **0.705**, strongly positive direct matching structure, and coherent copying-output weights.

## Reasoning

The shift-like readers and multiple induction-like circuits strongly favor **as-is text**. Shuffling would largely destroy the sequential regularities these circuits appear organized to exploit.

Corpus identification is much weaker. The substantial character subspace disfavors romaji somewhat. Multiple copying circuits make **Python** my narrow preference: repeated identifiers and code fragments provide particularly useful short-context repetition. English can also produce these structures, however. I have **not** identified keywords, particular characters, or indentation directly.

## Observations

**The strongest evidence is for ordered text, with short-range positional heads and later induction-like circuits. Corpus identification is substantially less certain.**

For the numerical evidence below, define the static weight products
\[
A_{\ell h}=D_\ell^\top W_{q,\ell h}^\top W_{k,\ell h}D_\ell/8,\qquad
B_{\ell h}=P W_{o,\ell h}W_{v,\ell h}D_\ell,
\]
where \(P=I-\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top/384\) and \(D_\ell=\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{ln1\_w.\ell})P\). These are matrix products, **not layer evaluations**.

- **A positional shift pair:** L0H1 and L0H5 have respectively **87.2% and 92.3%** of their raw QK energy outside the leading 27-dimensional shared value-read subspace. In a whitened 20-dimensional subspace, L0H1 aligns with the **square** of L0H5’s polar factor: cosine **0.642**, versus **0.071** with its first power. Removing the token-read proxy preserves this result (**0.649**). This suggests one-step and two-step positional retrieval, although the missing position embeddings prevent establishing absolute lags.
- **A pooling head:** L0H4 has \(\|A\|_F=\mathbf{0.009}\), versus **0.878** and **0.970** for L0H1/H5, but \(\|B\|_F=\mathbf{17.158}\). Its leading OV singular values are **13.877, 9.644, 2.507**. This strongly suggests broad, low-dimensional aggregation.
- **Induction-like connections:** Define \(c(A,B)=\operatorname{tr}(AB)/\|AB\|_*\). Connections from the likely previous-character head L0H5 score **0.212** into L2H1, **0.179** into L3H1, and **0.187** into L3H5. L2H2’s writes have still stronger connections into L3H1 (**0.288**) and L3H5 (**0.390**). These are substantial matching signatures, not proof of copying behavior.
- **Only weak corpus evidence:** `W_proj.3` has substantial singular values through many dimensions: \(s_2=\mathbf{20.293}\), \(s_{25}=\mathbf{10.769}\), \(s_{28}=\mathbf{7.929}\). Together with the early value spectra, this does not suggest an especially restricted character repertoire. That weakly disfavors romaji; spectral rank is not a literal vocabulary count.

## Heads

Labels are tentative. **“Unclear” means that these weight-only measurements do not distinguish the requested behaviors.**

L0H0: **unclear** — low-rank QK; its two leading OV modes dominate, but neither lag nor attention span is established.  
L0H1: **local** — strong square-of-L0H5 positional signature; likely retrieves roughly two characters back.  
L0H2: **unclear** — mixed content/position structure; positive symmetric QK modes do not distinguish self-attention from nearby retrieval.  
L0H3: **unclear** — substantial negative symmetric positional modes, without a reliable lag signature.  
L0H4: **broad** — exceptionally weak QK product, strong low-rank OV product; best pooling candidate.  
L0H5: **previous** — strong position-dominated rotational structure; likely the elementary shift underlying L0H1.

L1H0: **unclear** — 34.2% of key-side QK energy lies in L0H4’s leading write subspace; positional dependence, but unknown span.  
L1H1: **unclear** — corresponding positional-key fraction 62.7%; insufficient evidence for a particular lag.  
L1H2: **unclear** — positional-key fraction 63.1%; no strong predecessor-matching signature.  
L1H3: **unclear** — positional-key fraction 67.8%; clearly uses the aggregation head’s features, but its retrieval range is unresolved.  
L1H4: **unclear** — positional-key fraction 64.5%; positional routing does not establish locality.  
L1H5: **unclear** — positional-key fraction 52.5%; predecessor composition is comparatively weak.

L2H0: **unclear** — distributed QK structure; no distinctive shift or induction connection found.  
L2H1: **copy** — strongest L2 connection to L0H5’s writes: \(c=0.212\), consistent with predecessor matching.  
L2H2: **unclear** — its writes strongly support later matching circuits, but that does not establish where this head itself attends.  
L2H3: **unclear** — strongest positive composition is with the pooling head, not the likely previous-character head.  
L2H4: **unclear** — mixed positional/content structure; no discriminating lag or copying signature.  
L2H5: **unclear** — weaker QK and strong OV products, but insufficient evidence to distinguish pooling from selective retrieval.

L3H0: **unclear** — no strong induction connection; remaining products do not establish attention span.  
L3H1: **copy** — matching connections through L0H5 (\(c=0.179\)) and L2H2 (\(0.288\)).  
L3H2: **unclear** — no clear positional-shift or predecessor-matching signature.  
L3H3: **unclear** — relatively weak QK and strong OV make pooling plausible, but do not establish broad attention.  
L3H4: **unclear** — no sufficiently distinctive static signature among the requested categories.  
L3H5: **copy** — strongest induction-like candidate: \(c=0.390\) through L2H2, plus \(0.187\) through L0H5.

## Reasoning

The paired positional shifts and later predecessor-matching connections make **as-is training much more plausible than line shuffling**. Shuffling preserves useful line-level statistics, but largely destroys the sequential regularities these circuits appear designed to exploit.

I weakly favor **English**, with Python a close alternative. The substantial character-related subspaces weigh somewhat against romaji’s more restricted letter usage. However, I have not recovered labeled characters or a decisive English-versus-Python signature; the corpus choice is a best judgment, not an identification established by the weights.

claude.final:
**Observations:**
- **Method:** I used only products, decompositions and ICA on the weights. There was no softmax, LayerNorm or ReLU applied to any input. The offset profiles below are cosine sums over eigenmodes of Q^T K, and they assume L0H5 sits at offset 1 and that all modes have equal amplitude.
- **Position code:** L0H1 and L0H5 share a positional subspace (top-20 Q+K overlap 0.63, under 0.25 for the other L0 head pairs). W_q/W_k have rank about 40, and token-subspace energy is only 0.10–0.25.
    - Q^T K has complex eigenvalues with magnitude up to 16.
    - On shared planes, the phase in L0H1 is about 2–2.5× the phase in L0H5: 34°→87°, 51°→113°, 79°→178°, 115°→233°.
    - With those phases as frequencies, L0H5 peaks at offset 1 (scores 4 / 17 / 4 at offsets 0, 1, 2).
    - L0H1 peaks at offsets 2–3 (−3.3, 3.6, 13.1, 7.2, −2.7).
    - Modal gains are 16 and 12 here, against at most 1.0 in other L0 heads and at most 0.7 in L1–L3.
- **Unlearned head:** L0H4 has Q/K norms of 2.2 and 2.6, and random init predicts 2.22. Its score form is about 0.01, so it is a plain running mean. W_v/W_o are still large (W_o sv 5.6, 4.6). The top two W_k.1 directions (sv 11.0, 9.4) read this output.
- **Tokens:** ICA of W_fc.0 inside the top-30 W_v.0 subspace gives 27 stable sparse axes (kurtosis 41–400), plus 3 weak ones. The same axes stay sparse in the L0H1 and L0H5 slots, so they appear to be real characters. They carry no letter labels.
    - All 27 seem to be in use, with V gains well above init.
    - Copy maps from L3H1 and L3H5 agree per token. Cosine averages 0.67, against 0.18 rms off-diagonal, and only token 7 (0.25) comes close to the noise level.
- **Copy structure:** I scored same-token matches between query and key, using character slots c (current), p (previous, via L0H5) and b (2–3 back, via L0H1).

| Head | c>p | p>b |
|---|---|---|
| L2H1 | +16.8 | +20.3 |
| L3H1 | +15.0 | +11.4 |
| L3H5 | +17.1 | +20.0 |

  - Under the same score, L3H0 reaches only +5.8 on c>p.
  - L3H1 and L3H5 write 0.32 and 0.40 of their W_o energy into the output subspace of W_proj.3, against 0.15–0.18 for the other L3 heads.
- **L2H2 differs:** p>c +14.9 and b>p +13.2 are satisfied automatically at j = i−1, and c>p is −7.2.

**Heads:**
- L0H0: broad; token-gated, no shift modes (max modal gain 1.03).
- L0H1: local; peak at 2–3 back, phases about 2–2.5× L0H5.
- L0H2: broad; low confidence. Keys and values favour token 23 (probably space), with little distance dependence.
- L0H3: broad; low confidence. Token-class matching, modal gain 0.78.
- L0H4: broad; Q/K at init, so uniform attention over the context.
- L0H5: previous; sharp peak at offset 1.
- L1H0: broad; low confidence. No alignment signal, c>c −10.9, weakest score form in L1 (0.64).
- L1H1: local; b>p +5.7, p>c +3.0, c>c −21.1.
- L1H2: local; b>p +7.9, p>c −6.9, suggesting about 2 back.
- L1H3: local; b>p +8.5.
- L1H4: local; b>p +6.9, p>c −5.1.
- L1H5: local; weak, b>p +3.2, c>c −19.9.
- L2H0: local; weak, b>p +5.5.
- L2H1: copy; c>p +16.8, p>b +20.3.
- L2H2: local; content alignment at j = i−1 (p>c +14.9, b>p +13.2), c>p −7.2, so not induction.
- L2H3: local; b>p +9.4.
- L2H4: unclear; b>b +5.7, p>b +4.5, nothing decisive.
- L2H5: broad; low confidence. All |z| ≤ 4.2, weakest score form in L2 (1.65).
- L3H0: copy; weaker, c>p +5.8, b>b +9.1, cosine to copy map 0.31.
- L3H1: copy; c>p +15.0, cosine to copy map 0.91.
- L3H2: unclear; all |z| ≤ 2.7.
- L3H3: broad; smallest Q/K (10.5), weakest score form (1.05), largest V/W_o.
- L3H4: unclear; all |z| ≤ 2.6.
- L3H5: copy; c>p +17.1, p>b +20.0, p>p and b>b +26, cosine to copy map 0.91.

**Reasoning:**
- **Order:** This is the firm conclusion. Separate heads for offset 1 and offsets 2–3 would be pointless if characters within a line were exchangeable. Induction with a one-step shift (c>p, p>b) would be useless too, because shuffled text has nothing to copy forward.
- **Against romaji:** Hepburn romaji should leave l, q, v and x nearly unused, so about 24 active tokens. I see 27 with similar use. The cur→next table is also not dominated by a five-vowel alternation (top mode holds 20% of the variance). One finding points the other way: L0H1 and L0H5 keys are dominated by a five-token class (2, 13, 7, 6, 5). I first read that as vowels, but it is unconfirmed, and frequency-like measures don't support it.
- **English over Python:** This is a weaker call.
    - Copy heads barely use token 23, which has the lowest match weight and a copy cosine of 0.35. Python indentation should depend heavily on copying spaces.
    - L1 has no copy heads, although Python's repeated identifiers should favour them.
    - No token behaves like a frequent newline, and I found no line-structure head.
    - Against that, some evidence is neutral or slightly favours Python. The letter-frequency curve fits Python slightly better (0.966 vs 0.948).
- **Tests that gave no clear answer:**
    - Cipher-style matching against short sample texts I wrote from memory barely beat shuffled nulls. English led by only a small margin (0.384 vs null about 0.32).
    - A test of whether space can follow space had no power.
    - Only one bigram cleared the null: token 15→5 (z = 5.8), which looks like q→u or a similar forced pair, but that is unconfirmed.

import numpy as np, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA
from scipy.stats import kurtosis, skew

hd=lambda n,j,l=0: W[f'{n}.{l}'][64*j:64*j+64]
oh=lambda j,l=0: W[f'W_o.{l}'][:,64*j:64*j+64]
D0=W['ln1_w.0']; D2=W['ln2_w.0']; D3=W['ln1_w.3']
S=np.vstack([hd('W_v',1),hd('W_v',5)])
u,s,vt=np.linalg.svd(S,full_matrices=False); Th=vt[:28]
Tb=(Th/D0)
R=(W['W_fc.0']*D2)@Tb.T
rn=np.linalg.norm(R,axis=1); act=rn>4
ica=FastICA(n_components=28,whiten='unit-variance',max_iter=8000,tol=1e-6,random_state=0,fun='logcosh')
Y=ica.fit_transform(R[act])
tau=ica.components_.copy()            # 28x28, tau[c] token coordinate in Th basis
print('kurt',kurtosis(Y,axis=0).round(1))
sg=np.sign(skew(Y,axis=0)); tau=tau*sg[:,None]; Y=Y*sg
tau/=np.linalg.norm(tau,axis=1,keepdims=True)
# strength measures
Vs=[hd('W_v',1),hd('W_v',5)]
print('active neurons with Y>3 per token',(Y>3).sum(0)); print('Y<-3',(Y<-3).sum(0))

print('|V5 tau|',np.linalg.norm(hd('W_v',5)@Th.T@tau.T,axis=0).round(2))
# token->output maps through L3 copy heads

    print('H',j,'norm per token',np.linalg.norm(Mh[j],axis=0).round(1))
c=lambda A,B:(A/np.linalg.norm(A,axis=0)).T@(B/np.linalg.norm(B,axis=0))
print('diag cos M1 vs M5',np.diag(c(Mh[1],Mh[5])).round(2))
X=c(Mh[1],Mh[5]); off=X[~np.eye(28,dtype=bool)]; print('offdiag mean/std',off.mean().round(3),off.std().round(3))
print('M1 svd',np.linalg.svd(Mh[1],compute_uv=False)[[0,5,10,20,26]].round(1),'M5 svd',np.linalg.svd(Mh[5],compute_uv=False)[[0,5,10,20,26]].round(1))

def norm(t):
    out=[]
    for line in t.lower().split('\n'):
        m=re.match(r' *',line); lead=m.group(0); rest=line[len(lead):]
        rest=re.sub(r'[^a-z ]',' ',rest); rest=re.sub(r' +',' ',rest).rstrip()

def qap(Z,Ref,tlimit,seed=0):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); best=(-1e9,None); N=28; t0=time.time()

    return best

claude_r1.final:
**Observations:**

*Caveats*
- No letters could be labelled. Matching the weights to bigram tables I typed from memory did not beat a shuffled null, so that decoding gave no reliable labels.
- The head labels come from bilinear forms and spectra, not from observed attention. Lags are relative, and I set H5 to lag 1 as the natural reading.
- Runs 40–46 clipped or thresholded `W_fc.0` projections onto token directions to tabulate neuron tuning. Run 32 picked the best-tuned neurons and weighted `W_proj` columns by their projections. Neither was a forward pass, since there was no LayerNorm, softmax or `W_proj` after a ReLU. The clipping does come close to rule 1, though, so discount any corpus evidence that rests on it (the double-letter and "many followers" points below).

*Characters and output*
- `W_v.0` H1 and H5 share a read subspace of about 28 dimensions. Stacked singular values fall from 3.02 to 1.11 and 1.0, then reach background at about 0.9. These two heads put 89% and 86% of their V energy there.
- `W_q.0` and `W_k.0` in those heads have only 7–22% of their energy in that subspace. They read position (about 40–45 extra dimensions) and copy characters by relative position.
- ICA on `W_fc.0` gave stable single-character detector neurons, with kurtosis 11–129, for 27 axes. The 28th axis is weak (kurtosis 3.6).
- `W_proj.3` has exactly 27 dense output directions (singular values 20.3 down to 7.9, background 2.7). It also has a few sparse directions on coordinates 273, 123, 146 and 307, which probably control gain through the final LayerNorm.

*Relative position*
- The H1 and H5 forms in layer 0 nearly commute (relative commutator 0.09).
- Their shared modes have complex phases, with H1's about 2.2 times H5's, which fits lags of 1 and 2.

*Position channel*

## Observations

These are **weight-based hypotheses, not measured attention patterns**.

- **L0H3 looks like an offset-routing head.** Its \(W_q^\top W_k/8\) has stable rank **14.93**, unlike the nearly rank-one L0H1/H2/H4/H5. After incorporating LN scales, it has substantial complex eigenvalue pairs, including **\(0.1366\pm0.1327i\)**. Its dominant QK and OV-input subspaces are almost orthogonal: top-eight overlap **0.010–0.011**. This suggests position-based selection carrying character information.
- **L0H0 also looks positional:** approximately **79%/82%** of its scaled QK query/key energy lies in the position-like subspace identified from L0H3.
- **L3H3 has a distinctive induction-compatible connection to L0H3.** For their scaled QK–OV composition, restricted to L0H3’s leading read directions, trace/Frobenius norm is **2.730**, versus **−0.597 to 0.551** for the other L3 heads. Its symmetric part has positive/negative eigenvalue sums **0.4513/−0.0362**. This supports matching information previously transported by L0H3.
- Several heads share strong, low-dimensional routing machinery. For example, `ln1_b.1[39]=-1.5676`, `[58]=1.3651`, `[99]=-1.3355`; L1 query-bias-induced key directions have pairwise cosines **0.823–0.873**. These establish shared routing features, **not their attention distances**.
- The relatively concentrated early value spectra weakly favor a restricted, unevenly used alphabet. However, clustering did **not** recover convincing labeled characters or a clear vowel–consonant structure.

## Heads

Here, \(A\) denotes the LN-scale-adjusted QK matrix; quoted stable ranks without that qualification refer to raw QK.

L0H0: **local** — tentative; strong positional-subspace overlap and a multidimensional value channel suggest nearby-character routing.  
L0H1: **unclear** — QK stable rank 1.28; OV closely resembles H2, but no distance is established.  
L0H2: **unclear** — QK stable rank 1.36; OV cosine with H1 is 0.801, indicating shared low-dimensional machinery.  
L0H3: **previous** — strongest candidate; position-like rotational QK structure separated from its character-carrying value directions. Exact offset remains inferred.  
L0H4: **unclear** — QK stable rank 1.56; shared low-rank output directions do not distinguish local from distant routing.  
L0H5: **unclear** — weakest L0 QK norm, 0.210, but strongest OV norm, 29.436; consistent with coarse aggregation or a reference-position mechanism.

L1H0: **unclear** — strong shared key preference; bias-derived key coefficient norm 3.975, without an identified lag.  
L1H1: **unclear** — corresponding norm 3.689; no convincing predecessor-matching composition.  
L1H2: **unclear** — corresponding norm 3.051; predominantly shared routing structure.  
L1H3: **unclear** — corresponding norm 3.390; positional range cannot be recovered from this alone.  
L1H4: **unclear** — corresponding norm 2.328; particularly weak direct matching composition with L0H3.  
L1H5: **unclear** — corresponding norm 3.895; shares the common key preference, but its range is unresolved.

L2H0: **unclear** — scaled QK stable rank 5.61; strong shared key-bias component, not a demonstrated lag.  
L2H1: **unclear** — scaled QK stable rank 13.91; negligible direct predecessor-matching score.  
L2H2: **unclear** — scaled QK stable rank 11.02; mixed content/routing structure without clear induction evidence.  
L2H3: **unclear** — scaled QK stable rank 10.45; weaker alignment with the common key preference.  
L2H4: **unclear** — scaled QK stable rank 7.43; some positive predecessor composition, insufficient for a copy label.  
L2H5: **unclear** — scaled QK stable rank 13.54; negligible direct predecessor-matching score.

L3H0: **unclear** — predecessor-composition trace/norm −0.597; not the positive matching signature seen in H3.  
L3H1: **unclear** — corresponding statistic −0.090; attention range remains unidentified.  
L3H2: **unclear** — corresponding statistic 0.184; weak evidence for direct induction.  
L3H3: **copy** — strongest induction candidate; distinctive positive matching composition with the likely previous-character head.  
L3H4: **unclear** — weak QK alongside strong OV suggests aggregation, but does not establish broad attention.  
L3H5: **unclear** — predecessor-composition statistic −0.152; neither a clear copy circuit nor an identified positional offset.

## Reasoning

The likely previous-character circuit and its later induction-compatible reader favor **ordered text** over line-shuffled text. They suggest short-range character processing plus retrieval useful for repeating earlier sequences.

**Romaji is my weaker corpus preference:** the concentrated early character-information channels are compatible with its uneven alphabet usage and strong local spelling constraints. English remains quite plausible; nothing recovered identifies Japanese syllables or excludes Python decisively. The corpus probabilities therefore reflect a tentative judgment, not a calibrated classifier.

## Observations:

All measurements below are **weight-only**, not forward passes. Head labels are hypotheses; attention distances cannot be verified without the missing embeddings and activations.

For compactness, define
\[
A=G W_q^\top W_kG/8,\qquad B=W_oW_vG,\qquad
r=G W_k^\top W_q\,\mathrm{ln1_b}/8,
\]
where \(G=\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{ln1_w})\), using each head’s slices. Thus \(A\) is its bilinear score matrix, \(B\) its value/output product, and \(r\) a key-dependent affine coefficient.

- **L0H3 stands out as a directional positional head.** Its \(W_q,W_k\) norms are **14.141, 14.661**, substantially above the other L0 heads. Its unscaled QK product has complex eigenvalues including **\(0.724\pm0.691i\)** and **\(0.446\pm0.842i\)**. The leading 16-dimensional Q/K subspaces overlap strongly (**0.620**), whereas Q/V overlap is only **0.0177**. This supports position-controlled transport of different, likely character-related information.
- **Several L0 heads construct shared low-dimensional signals.** Coordinates **21,39,58,99,184** contain **94.0%, 94.2%, 87.8%, 97.0%** of \(B\)’s squared norm for H1,H2,H4,H5. These coordinates have no intrinsic semantic labels.
- **Later heads strongly read those shared signals.** For example, `ln1_b.1[39]=-1.5676`, `[58]=1.3651`, and `[99]=-1.3355`. All six L1 heads have positive \(r_{21}\), ranging from **2.008 to 3.627**. This is consistent with a shared positional/recency mechanism, although it does not establish its meaning conclusively.
- **L3H3 has a distinctive induction-compatible connection to L0H3.** Let \(T\) contain the leading 20 right-singular directions of L0H3’s scaled value matrix. For
  \[
  C=T^\top A_{3,3}B_{0,3}T,
  \]
  \(\operatorname{tr}(C)/\|C\|_F=\mathbf{2.860}\). Signed/permuted-coordinate controls had standard deviation **0.234** and maximum **0.682** across 1,000 trials. This is strong evidence of learned matching through the earlier transport circuit.
- **The corpus-specific evidence is weaker.** The leading 24 singular directions of `W_proj.3` contain **92.14%** of its squared norm; directions 25–28 add only **1.62%**. This is compatible with a comparatively restricted frequently used alphabet, but is **not** a recovered character count.

## Heads:

The “local” assignments below largely depend on the tentative recency interpretation of the shared channel.

L0H0: **local** — Its positional-subspace score matrix resembles a higher power of L0H3’s directional factor more than the first power; compatible with a longer short offset.

L0H1: **unclear** — Almost rank-two score/output structure; 94.0% of output-product energy enters the shared coordinates. Boundary selection and positional bookkeeping remain alternatives.

L0H2: **unclear** — One score singular mode carries 90.8% of energy; 94.2% of output energy enters the shared coordinates. Distance is unresolved.

L0H3: **previous** — Strongest predecessor candidate: high-rank directional QK structure, separated positional and value subspaces, and the downstream induction-compatible connection.

L0H4: **unclear** — Dominant rank-one score component and 87.8% shared-coordinate output concentration; insufficient evidence for a particular attention distance.

L0H5: **broad** — Very weak score product, with leading singular value **0.032**, but strong low-rank value transport (**16.282, 8.786**); consistent with context aggregation.

L1H0: **local** — Strong shared-channel preference: \(r_{21}=3.627\); key column 21 contains 30.1% of score-product energy.

L1H1: **local** — \(r_{21}=3.352\), with 32.5% key-column-21 energy; closely resembles the other L1 recency candidates.

L1H2: **local** — \(r_{21}=2.769\), with 36.4% key-column-21 energy.

L1H3: **local** — \(r_{21}=3.079\), with 36.4% key-column-21 energy.

L1H4: **local** — \(r_{21}=2.008\), with 34.8% key-column-21 energy; weaker shared preference than most L1 heads.

L1H5: **local** — \(r_{21}=3.563\), with 31.9% key-column-21 energy.

L2H0: **local** — Retains the shared mechanism strongly: \(r_{21}=1.815\), with 15.4% key-column-21 energy.

L2H1: **local** — \(r_{21}=1.682\); substantial shared-channel preference, but more distributed content-sensitive score structure.

L2H2: **local** — \(r_{21}=1.411\); compatible with content-conditioned local retrieval.

L2H3: **local** — Lower-confidence assignment: the shared preference remains, \(r_{21}=0.803\), but is weaker.

L2H4: **local** — Strongest L2 shared-channel preference, \(r_{21}=2.069\); supports recency-sensitive retrieval.

L2H5: **local** — \(r_{21}=1.859\), without a distinctive positive L0H3 matching composition.

L3H0: **local** — Residual shared-channel preference, \(r_{21}=0.408\); the tested predecessor-matching composition is negative, unlike L3H3.

L3H1: **unclear** — Weaker shared-channel preference, \(r_{21}=0.181\), and no strong tested induction signature; local versus broader retrieval remains unresolved.

L3H2: **local** — \(r_{21}=0.382\); retains the common positional mechanism without L3H3’s matching signature.

L3H3: **copy** — Strong positive matching through L0H3: projected composition trace/norm **2.860**, far beyond the coordinate-randomization controls.

L3H4: **broad** — Little shared-channel preference, \(r_{21}=0.028\), combined with large value/output singular values **21.271, 17.680**; favors an aggregation interpretation.

L3H5: **local** — \(r_{21}=0.416\), with no comparable positive predecessor-matching signature.

## Reasoning:

**Intact order is strongly favored.** A directional character-transport circuit followed by an induction-compatible matching circuit is useful for ordered sequences and repetition. Randomly shuffling each line largely removes those predictive relationships, although it preserves line-level composition and boundaries.

**Romaji is my best, less-confident corpus judgment.** The comparatively concentrated character-related geometry and substantial short-context machinery fit a restricted, regular romanized orthography. English remains a serious alternative; the spectra do not identify letters, vowels, words, or language directly. I find less positive evidence specifically favoring Python.

## Observations

These are **weight-based hypotheses**, not measured attention patterns.

I used \(A=(W_qDP)^T(W_kDP)/8\) and \(B=W_oW_vDP\), where \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\text{ln1_w})\) and \(P\) removes the constant direction. These are matrix products, not forward passes.

- **L0H3 looks like positional transport.** Its unadjusted QK stable rank is **14.93**, versus **1.28–2.62** for the other first-layer heads. Its QK eigenvalues include **\(0.724\pm0.691i\)** and **\(0.446\pm0.842i\)**: substantial rotational/asymmetric structure, consistent with an offset rather than simple same-character matching.
- **L3H3 has a particularly strong induction signature through L0H3.** In a fixed, weight-derived 22-dimensional early-value read subspace, the key-composition product has trace/nuclear-norm **0.782**. Corresponding compositions through the other first-layer heads range from **−0.168 to 0.072**. Signed-permutation controls gave mean approximately **0**, standard deviation **0.064**, maximum **0.307**. This strongly supports a specific matching circuit, though it does not establish its behavioral effect.
- **L0H5 looks like a diffuse summary channel.** Its adjusted QK Frobenius norm is only **0.034**, while its adjusted OV leading singular values are **16.278, 8.778, 2.833**.
- **Many later heads read that shared channel.** Its leading three output directions capture **79.8–86.1%** of the bias-induced key-vector energy in layer 1. This establishes shared routing machinery—not its attention distance.
- First-layer heads **H1/H2/H4** are closely related: H1–H2 adjusted OV cosine **0.925**, H1–H4 **0.869**. A shared structural or boundary-related role is plausible, but no character identity is established.

## Heads

Below, \(r\) denotes the fraction of the bias-induced key-vector energy in L0H5’s leading three output directions.

L0H0: **local** — tentative; 41.6% of QK energy lies within the positional-candidate subspace; exact offset unresolved.  
L0H1: **unclear** — adjusted QK stable rank 1.12; strongly shares H2’s value/output circuit.  
L0H2: **unclear** — adjusted QK stable rank 1.10; likely a related structural selector, not an identifiable lag.  
L0H3: **previous** — strongest candidate: asymmetric positional structure and the specific downstream induction composition.  
L0H4: **unclear** — adjusted QK stable rank 1.24; resembles H1/H2, but attention span is unestablished.  
L0H5: **broad** — tentative; exceptionally weak QK product paired with a strong, low-dimensional OV summary.

L1H0: **unclear** — \(r=0.853\); strong shared key selection, insufficient evidence for a particular distance.  
L1H1: **unclear** — \(r=0.853\); position/structure-channel dependence does not distinguish local from broad.  
L1H2: **unclear** — \(r=0.851\); no strong previous-head induction signature.  
L1H3: **unclear** — \(r=0.854\); shared routing dominates the bias-induced key preference.  
L1H4: **unclear** — \(r=0.798\); similar machinery, but neither lag nor spread is recoverable here.  
L1H5: **unclear** — \(r=0.861\); particularly strong shared-channel dependence, without a demonstrated span.

L2H0: **unclear** — \(r=0.832\); substantial shared-channel selection, weak induction composition.  
L2H1: **unclear** — \(r=0.824\); higher-rank QK structure, but no reliable distance assignment.  
L2H2: **unclear** — \(r=0.787\); mixed routing features rather than a distinctive copy signature.  
L2H3: **unclear** — \(r=0.615\); less dominated by the shared channel, still behaviorally ambiguous.  
L2H4: **unclear** — \(r=0.830\); strong shared-channel dependence does not establish locality.  
L2H5: **unclear** — \(r=0.856\); no convincing previous-character or induction-specific composition.

L3H0: **unclear** — \(r=0.692\); L0H3 key-composition score is negative, −0.175.  
L3H1: **unclear** — \(r=0.475\); neither a strong positional-offset nor induction signature.  
L3H2: **unclear** — \(r=0.625\); L0H3 key-composition score only 0.035.  
L3H3: **copy** — strongest classification: specific L0H3 key-composition score 0.782, versus query-composition −0.398.  
L3H4: **broad** — tentative; relatively weak adjusted QK norm 0.622, little shared-channel dependence, strong OV singular value 29.438 unadjusted.  
L3H5: **unclear** — \(r=0.721\); L0H3 key-composition score −0.036, not an induction signature.

## Reasoning

The strongest evidence favors **ordered text**: an early offset-like transport circuit feeding a specific late induction candidate. Shuffling within lines substantially reduces the usefulness of retrieving continuations of earlier character sequences.

Corpus identification is much weaker. I modestly favor **Python** because the combination of structural/positional specialization and continuation retrieval fits structured lines and repeated identifiers. English remains a substantial alternative; these weights do **not** identify indentation, keywords, or particular letters directly. The spectral analyses also did not provide a compelling restricted-alphabet signature for romaji.

Thus my best account is **local character transport, shared contextual summaries/routing, and late continuation matching**, with most individual attention spans unresolved.

def describe(a):
    a = np.asarray(a, dtype=np.float64)
    return np.array([a.mean(), a.std(), a.min(), np.median(a), a.max()])

print("QK_sym: symmetric-part squared-norm fraction; QK_tr: trace/Frobenius norm")
print("OV_s: top 5 singular values; OV_tr: trace/Frobenius norm")

        pa = sa / sa.sum()

        ea = np.linalg.eigvalsh((A + A.T)/2)
        eb = np.linalg.eigvals(V @ O)
        print(f"L{l}H{j}",
              "normQKVO", np.round([np.linalg.norm(t) for t in [Q,K,V,O]], 3),
              "QK_s", sa[:5].round(3), "QK_er", round(er,2),
              "QK_sym", round(np.linalg.norm((A+A.T)/2)**2/np.linalg.norm(A)**2,3),
              "QK_tr", round(np.trace(A)/np.linalg.norm(A),3),
              "QK_sym_ext", np.round([ea[0],ea[-1]],3),
              "OV_s", sb[:5].round(3),
              "OV_tr", round(np.trace(B)/np.linalg.norm(B),3),
              "OV_eig", round(np.trace(B)/(np.abs(eb).sum()+1e-30),3),

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits
threadpool_limits(4)
np.set_printoptions(precision=2,suppress=True,linewidth=200)

def rd(M,g):
    X=M.astype(float)*g
    return X-X.mean(axis=1,keepdims=True)

F=W["W_fc.0"].astype(float)
G=rd(F,W["ln2_w.0"])
s=slice(192,256)
O=W["W_o.0"][:,s].astype(float)
V=rd(W["W_v.0"][s],W["ln1_w.0"])
Q=rd(W["W_q.0"][s],W["ln1_w.0"])
K=rd(W["W_k.0"][s],W["ln1_w.0"])
uo,so,_=np.linalg.svd(O,full_matrices=False)
_,sp,pt=np.linalg.svd(np.vstack([Q,K]),full_matrices=False)
ctrl=np.eye(384)[:,[21,39,58,99,184]]
mask=np.linalg.norm(F,axis=1)>1.3
G=G[mask]
GP=G@O@V
variants={}
for name,blocks in [
    ("O64", [uo,ctrl]),
    ("O32_position24", [uo[:,:32],pt[:24].T,ctrl]),
    ("O64_position32", [uo,pt[:32].T,ctrl]),
]:
    U,sv,_=np.linalg.svd(np.hstack(blocks),full_matrices=False)
    U=U[:,sv>1e-6]
    C=G-(G@U)@U.T
    variants[name]=C

results=[]
for name,C in variants.items():
    C=C-C.mean(axis=0,keepdims=True)
    u,ss,vt=np.linalg.svd(C,full_matrices=False)
    print(name,"spectrum",ss[:36].round(2))
    for r in [18,22,26,30]:
        X=u[:,:r]*ss[:r]
        X/=np.linalg.norm(X,axis=1,keepdims=True)+1e-20
        for k in [20,24,28]:
            km=KMeans(n_clusters=k,n_init=8,random_state=7).fit(X)
            score=float(silhouette_score(X,km.labels_))
            results.append((score,name,r,k,km.labels_))
results.sort(key=lambda x:x[0],reverse=True)
print("\nBest cluster fits (silhouette, construction, rank, number)")
print([(round(s,3),n,r,k) for s,n,r,k,_ in results[:12]])

score,name,r,k,lab=results[0]
C=variants[name]
cent=np.array([C[lab==i].mean(axis=0) for i in range(k)])
prev=np.array([GP[lab==i].mean(axis=0) for i in range(k)])
cent-=cent.mean(axis=0,keepdims=True)
prev-=prev.mean(axis=0,keepdims=True)
gram=cent@cent.T
reg=.08*np.trace(gram)/k
J=(prev@cent.T)@np.linalg.inv(gram+reg*np.eye(k))
J-=J.mean(axis=0,keepdims=True)
J-=J.mean(axis=1,keepdims=True)
J/=np.sqrt(np.mean(J**2))
print("\nBest-fit cluster counts",np.bincount(lab,minlength=k))
print("Regularized cross-channel cluster coefficient matrix (weight algebra only)")
print(J.round(1))
print("\nSymmetrized coefficient eigenvalues")
ev,U=np.linalg.eigh((J+J.T)/2)
print(ev.round(2))
vec=U[:,0]
part=vec>0
print("Most-negative-eigenvector partition:",np.where(part)[0],np.where(~part)[0])
print("Four block means:",[[round(float(J[np.ix_(a,b)].mean()),3) for b in [part,~part]] for a in [part,~part]])

print("\nTop-3 previous-channel coefficient clusters for each current-read cluster")
for i in range(k):
    ix=np.argsort(-J[i])[:3]
    print(i,int(np.sum(lab==i)),[(int(j),round(float(J[i,j]),2)) for j in ix])

## Observations

**The strongest evidence concerns context use, not corpus identity.** These are weight-based hypotheses; no attention patterns were evaluated.

Define \(A\) as each head’s QK product, incorporating the learned LayerNorm scales and mean-centering, and \(B\) as its similarly adjusted OV product.

- **L0H3 is a distinctive positional-routing candidate.** Its raw `W_q.0[192:256]` and `W_k.0[192:256]` have Frobenius norms **14.141 and 14.661**. Its adjusted QK product has substantial complex eigenpairs, including **0.1366 ± 0.1327i**, unlike the predominantly low-rank other first-layer heads. This suggests an offset-selecting mechanism, plausibly previous-character attention.
- **L3H3 has a strong, directional connection to L0H3 consistent with induction.** On a weight-derived candidate content subspace, its key-composition score with L0H3 is **2.563**, versus **−0.971** for query composition. Randomizing the pairing of L0H3’s learned OV dimensions produced scores with mean **−0.018**, standard deviation **0.238**, and none exceeding the observed score in 1,000 trials. This establishes a specialized connection—not, by itself, its behavioral interpretation.
- **L0H5 looks aggregation-oriented:** adjusted QK norm **0.034**, versus **0.698** for L0H3, but adjusted OV norm **18.804**, versus **3.533**. Weak relative selectivity and strong writing suggest broad context aggregation.
- **Several heads share a low-dimensional control channel.** L0H1 and L0H2’s OV products have cosine similarity **0.925**. Their outputs emphasize coordinates 21, 39, 58 and 99. Related weights include `ln1_b.1[39] = −1.5676`, `[58] = 1.3651`, and `[99] = −1.3355`. These coordinates have no known character or position labels.
- **There is no decisive corpus fingerprint.** Neither the singular spectra nor the exploratory MLP-weight clustering securely identifies letters, Japanese syllable structure, or Python indentation.

## Heads

Here, \(a=\|A\|_F\). “Composition score” refers to the content-subspace key-composition diagnostic above. **“Unclear” does not mean inactive.**

| Head | Most likely | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| L0H0 | local | Shares substantial QK structure with L0H3’s routing subspace; \(a=0.293\). Tentative locality, not an identified lag. |
| L0H1 | unclear | Rank-one component carries 89.2% of QK energy; shared control-channel output does not establish attention range. |
| L0H2 | unclear | 90.9% rank-one QK energy; OV closely resembles L0H1, but no identifiable offset. |
| L0H3 | previous | Distinctive rotation-like QK structure and strong downstream induction-compatible connection. |
| L0H4 | unclear | 80.9% rank-one QK energy; another shared-control writer, with unresolved range. |
| L0H5 | broad | Exceptionally small QK norm, 0.034, paired with large OV norm, 18.804; aggregation is the best hypothesis. |
| L1H0 | unclear | Strong shared-control key dependence; composition score 0.548 is insufficient to establish induction or distance. |
| L1H1 | unclear | Shared control structure; composition score 0.366, without clear induction orientation. |
| L1H2 | unclear | Approximately 49% of QK energy involves the selected control coordinates on the key side; their positional meaning is unknown. |
| L1H3 | unclear | Strong control-key dependence; negligible direct induction signature, score 0.022. |
| L1H4 | unclear | Control-dependent routing; negative composition score −0.264 does not identify an alternative range. |
| L1H5 | unclear | Resembles other L1 control-dependent heads; composition score 0.443 remains inconclusive. |
| L2H0 | unclear | Distributed QK structure, \(a=1.631\); direct composition score only 0.076. |
| L2H1 | unclear | High-rank QK structure; composition score −0.045 gives no direct induction evidence. |
| L2H2 | unclear | Distributed routing weights; composition score 0.174 does not establish a context distance. |
| L2H3 | unclear | No distinctive offset or direct induction signature; composition score −0.112. |
| L2H4 | unclear | Substantial QK strength, \(a=2.215\), but composition evidence depends on the chosen subspace. |
| L2H5 | unclear | High-rank QK structure; weak direct composition score 0.135. |
| L3H0 | unclear | No positive L0H3 key-composition signature; score −0.464. Other contextual mechanisms remain possible. |
| L3H1 | unclear | Relatively weaker QK and stronger OV, but insufficient evidence to distinguish broad from selective attention. |
| L3H2 | unclear | Direct composition score 0.022; neither offset nor induction is established. |
| L3H3 | copy | Strong positive, asymmetric L0H3 key composition, robust across several weight-derived subspaces. |
| L3H4 | broad | Lowest final-layer QK norm, 0.622, and largest OV norm, 49.232; broad aggregation is tentative. |
| L3H5 | unclear | Distributed QK structure and no positive direct induction signature; score −0.080. |

## Reasoning

The likely **previous-character → induction** connection favors **as-is training**: it provides a mechanism for using ordered context to repeat earlier continuations. Together with the aggregation candidates, it suggests a mixture of short-range character processing and longer-range reuse.

**Corpus identification is much weaker.** All three unshuffled corpora reward those mechanisms. I give **English a slight, low-confidence lead**, with romaji close behind; the weights examined do not justify claiming that identifiable English words, Japanese syllables, or Python constructs were recovered. def bigram(txt,M=24):
    voc=[c for c,_ in sorted({c:txt.count(c) for c in set(txt)}.items(),key=lambda t:-t[1])][:M]
    while len(voc)<M: voc.append('?')
    idx={c:i for i,c in enumerate(voc)}
    C=np.zeros((M,M))
    for a,b in zip(txt,txt[1:]):
        if a in idx and b in idx: C[idx[a],idx[b]]+=1
    C=C+0.3
    p=C/C.sum(); L=np.log(p/np.outer(p.sum(1),p.sum(0))); np.fill_diagonal(L,0)
    return L,voc
def corr_score(E,L,pi,mask):
    X=L[np.ix_(pi,pi)][mask]; return np.corrcoef(E[mask],X)[0,1]
def sa(E,L,seed,steps=30000):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); M=L.shape[0]; perm=rng.permutation(M)
    mask=~np.eye(N,dtype=bool); Ez=E-E[mask].mean()
    def score(p): return (Ez*(L[np.ix_(p[:N],p[:N])]))[mask].sum()
    cur=score(perm); best=cur; bp=perm.copy()
    T0=abs(cur)/30+5
    for t in range(steps):
        T=T0*(1-t/steps)+1e-3
        i=rng.integers(N); j=rng.integers(M)
        if i==j: continue
        q=perm.copy(); q[i],q[j]=q[j],q[i]
        c=score(q)
        if c>cur or rng.random()<np.exp((c-cur)/T):
            perm=q; cur=c
            if c>best: best=c; bp=q.copy()
    return best,bp

def bigram(txt,M=25):
    voc=[c for c,_ in sorted({c:txt.count(c) for c in set(txt)}.items(),key=lambda t:-t[1])][:M]
    idx={c:i for i,c in enumerate(voc)}; M=len(voc)

    for a,b in zip(txt,txt[1:]):
        if a in idx and b in idx: C[idx[a],idx[b]]+=1
    p=(C+0.2)/(C+0.2).sum(); PMI=np.log(p/np.outer(p.sum(1),p.sum(0)))
    np.fill_diagonal(PMI,0)
    return PMI,voc
def sa(E,L,seed,steps):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); M=L.shape[0]
    Ez=E-E[mask].mean()
    perm=rng.permutation(M)
    def full(p):
        Lp=L[np.ix_(p[:N],p[:N])]; return float(((Ez*Lp)*mask).sum())
    cur=full(perm); best=cur; bp=perm.copy()
    T0=np.abs(Ez).sum()*L.std()/200; 
    for t in range(steps):
        Tm=T0*(1-t/steps)**2+1e-4
        i=rng.integers(N); j=rng.integers(M)
        if i==j: continue
        perm[i],perm[j]=perm[j],perm[i]
        c=full(perm)
        if c>=cur or rng.random()<np.exp((c-cur)/Tm): 
            cur=c
            if c>best: best=c; bp=perm.copy()
        else:
            perm[i],perm[j]=perm[j],perm[i]
    return best,bp

**Observations:**
- **Weights near init:** L0H1, H2, H4 and H5 have small q/k (L0H5 ‖q‖ = 2.6, ‖k‖ = 2.9, against init ≈ 2.2). L0H5 has large v and o (8.5, 9.6). Their top value directions lie in one 2-D plane, which is outside the token space and is shared with the top keys of L0H3 and L0H0, so it looks positional.
- **L0H3 is the only strong order-sensitive head:** ‖q‖ = 14.1, ‖k‖ = 14.7, rank about 34, and its Q and K span the same subspace (principal cosines 0.99). The eigenvalues of K Q^T are complex, with |λ| 1.53, 1.13, 1.09 at phases ±44°, ±39°, ±46°, rising to about ±160°. That is a rotation, meaning a causal shift. These planes are outside the token and MLP subspaces, and its W_v reads tokens instead.
- **Token recovery:** ICA on the 599 live rows of W_fc.0 (937 are dead) gives 23 stable token-like components. They survive changes of seed and rank, and their L0H3 images match independent ICA components in the "previous character" subspace (cosines up to 0.88). W_proj.3 has about 23 token output dimensions (s₁…s₂₃ = 22.2…8.2), and L3H3 writes about 2.0 into each of them, against about 0.8 for other heads.
- **Vowel class:** the first eigenvector of token similarity across layers isolates exactly five tokens, then a clear gap (−0.39, −0.34, −0.30, −0.29, −0.28, then −0.12).
- **Recency mask:** coordinates 21, 39, 58, 99 are written mainly by L0H5 (W_o rows 6.0, 5.3, 4.0, 3.9) and read almost only by keys (W_k.1 column norms 10.6, 7.8, 7.7, 10.1 against a median of 1.5; W_v columns ≈ 0–0.4; ln2_w.1[21] = 0.0). The ln1_b offsets (−1.57, 1.37, −1.34) centre this channel. Its gate Q·b→K is nearly identical across heads (cos ≥ 0.95). It weakens with depth (‖g‖ about 3.8 in L1, 1.8 in L2, 0.5 in L3) and is absent in L3H3 and L3H4. Its sign, inferred indirectly from the L0H3 rotation, favours recent positions.
- **Copy head:** in L3H3 the query on the current token matched against the key on the previous-character image scores trace-cosine +0.51. The reverse pairing scores −0.26, and the noise level is about 0.04. Its value head reads raw tokens more than any other L3 head does, and writes them into the output dimensions.

**Heads:**
- L0H0: local. Moderate q/k, avoids nearby positions in the L0H3 planes, value reads rarer tokens.
- L0H1: broad. Low-rank q/k, value reads the position plane.
- L0H2: broad. Same pattern as H1.
- L0H3: previous. Sharp rotation kernel, value reads tokens.
- L0H4: broad. Same pattern as H1.
- L0H5: broad. Almost no q/k, so nearly uniform attention, feeding the recency channel.
- L1H0: local. Gate 3.8, self-avoiding (token trace-cosine −0.47).
- L1H1: local. Gate 3.5; slight preference for the previous character (+0.14).
- L1H2: local. Gate 3.0.

def ref(t,ch,eps=0.3):
    i={c:k for k,c in enumerate(ch)}
    B=np.ones((len(ch),len(ch)))*eps
    for a,b in zip(t,t[1:]):
        if a in i and b in i: B[i[a],i[b]]+=1
    P=B/B.sum(1,keepdims=True)
    return np.log(P)
def search(M,Rlog,restarts,seed=0,fix=None):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); n=M.shape[0]

    bestv=-9;bestp=None
    free=[i for i in range(n) if fix is None or i!=fix[0]]
    for rs in range(restarts):
        p=rng.permutation(n)
        if fix is not None:
            j=int(np.where(p==fix[1])[0][0]); p[[j,fix[0]]]=p[[fix[0],j]]
        cur=(Mz*Rz[np.ix_(p,p)])[mask].sum(); imp=True
        while imp:
            imp=False
            for ia,a in enumerate(free):
                for b in free[ia+1:]:
                    p[[a,b]]=p[[b,a]]
                    v=(Mz*Rz[np.ix_(p,p)])[mask].sum()
                    if v>cur+1e-9: cur=v;imp=True

        if cur>bestv: bestv=cur;bestp=p.copy()
    return bestv/mask.sum(),bestp
